rules.title: Berkeley Coordinated Pricing Algorithm Prohibition (BMC Chapter 13.63; Ordinance No. 7,992-N.S.)
rules.requirement: Makes it unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide Berkeley landlords a coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels for residential units in Berkeley. It also makes it unlawful for landlords to use such an algorithm. A coordinated pricing algorithm is one that uses nonpublic Competitor Data to recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other lease terms in coordination between a Berkeley landlord and its competitors, including through a third-party vendor.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; each month and each unit is a separate violation; Competitor Data = nonpublic data on other landlords' properties less than 90 days old
rules.coverage_conditions: Sellers, licensors or providers of coordinated pricing algorithms to Berkeley landlords, and landlords setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley
rules.exemptions: (a) Products or reports that publish aggregated and anonymous rental data but do not recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other lease terms; (b) products used to set rent or income limits under government affordable housing guidelines; (c) information used for market research for project financing, appraisals, or research, testing or training for software development, provided Competitor Data is not an input to the model when a recommendation is calculated for a Berkeley landlord.
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use a coordinated pricing algorithm described in subsection A when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley. Each separate month that a violation exists or continues, and each separate residential dwelling unit for which the landlord used the coordinated pricing algorithm, shall constitute a separate and distinct violation.

rules.title: Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 13.78 – Tenant Screening Fee Disclosure and Renewal Fee Prohibition
rules.requirement: Before receiving a fee for a consumer credit report and application processing, an owner or agent must give the applicant a clear and conspicuous Tenant Screening Fee Rights Statement and a statement of the maximum fee cap under Civil Code 1950.6(b). This can be in the rental application or a separate disclosure. Owners also may not charge existing tenants any non-refundable fee to renew a tenancy, including fees tied to a roommate leaving or to adding or replacing a roommate.
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of residential rental property in Berkeley and their agents who charge screening/application fees. The renewal-fee ban protects existing tenants. The chapter applies to all residential rental agreements, including existing ones, regardless of contrary lease language.
rules.interaction: Coexists with state law: the local disclosure requirement references the state maximum screening fee cap under Civil Code 1950.6(b). Any lease provision that violates Chapter 13.78 is unenforceable.
rules.quoted_span: the owner must provide, either in the rental application or in a separate disclosure before receiving the fee, a clear and conspicuous tenant screening fee rights statement and a statement of the maximum fee cap permitted under

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance (as amended by Measure BB)
rules.requirement: Tenants in fully or partially covered units cannot be evicted without just cause. Eviction for nonpayment requires rent owed of at least one month of HUD Fair Market Rent. Tenants cannot be evicted for refusing to sign a substantially similar lease when a fixed-term lease expires. Eviction for breach of a material lease term requires four things: the term was mutually agreed, the breach caused substantial actual damage, the tenant's behavior was unreasonable, and a detailed notice to cease was given. Termination notices must include Rent Board advice and contact information. Landlords must file termination notices and summons/complaints with the Rent Board within 3 business days of service.
rules.key_value: Nonpayment eviction requires rental debt of at least 1 month of HUD Fair Market Rent (Oakland-Fremont, CA HUD Metro FMR) for an equivalent-size unit; notices must be filed with the Rent Board within 3 business days of service
rules.coverage_conditions: Units fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance. This includes pre-1980 multifamily units, single-family homes regardless of when the tenancy started, rooming houses, new construction after June 1980, most condominiums, and listed subsidized units.
rules.exemptions: Golden Duplex; units where the owner shares a kitchen or bath with the tenant, if the owner lived on the property when the tenancy started; tenancies started after Nov 7, 2018 on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied; university rental units such as dormitories; nonprofit cooperatives
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance; Measure BB (Berkeley Rent Ordinance)
rules.quoted_span: In Berkeley, tenants in units that are fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance cannot be evicted unless there is "just cause” (previously called “good cause”).

rules.title: BMC 13.106 – Prohibition on Termination Based on Criminal History
rules.requirement: Landlords may not refuse to rent to someone, or terminate a tenancy, based on criminal history.
rules.key_value: Administrative fines of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation
rules.coverage_conditions: Current or prospective tenants in Berkeley rental housing
rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing/Section 8 properties; owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record resides in one unit as their primary residence; units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back in per BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates
rules.interaction: Separate local chapter that coexists with the Rent Ordinance's just cause protections and references BMC 13.76.130 A.9.
rules.quoted_span: Refuse to rent or terminate a tenancy based on criminal history

rules.title: Ellis Implementation Ordinance – Relocation Assistance
rules.requirement: Owners must pay relocation assistance to tenants evicted so the owner can withdraw the property from the rental market under the Ellis Act. The amounts are the same as for owner move-in evictions and are indexed annually to CPI.
rules.key_value: Standard payment $19,413, plus an additional $6,471 for qualifying households (effective Jan 1, 2026; 1.5% CPI adjustment)
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants evicted for withdrawal of the property from the rental housing market (Ellis Act)
rules.interaction: Local ordinance implementing Ellis Act withdrawals. Payment amounts match the owner move-in relocation assistance under the Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance. The effective date reflects the 2026 adjusted amounts.
rules.quoted_span: The Ellis Implementation Ordinance requires the same relocation assistance payments for tenants evicted so the owner can remove a property from the rental housing market.

rules.title: Owner Move-In Relocation Assistance (Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance)
rules.requirement: Owners must pay relocation assistance to tenants evicted for owner move-in. The amount is adjusted each year by the 12-month CPI increase; for 2026 the adjustment is 1.5%.
rules.key_value: Standard payment $19,413, plus an additional $6,471 for qualifying households (effective Jan 1, 2026; 1.5% CPI-U San Francisco-Oakland-San Jose adjustment)
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants evicted for owner move-in
rules.interaction: Part of the same local rent/eviction ordinance as the just cause rule. The effective date reflects the 2026 adjusted payment amounts, not the original enactment. The Ellis Implementation Ordinance requires the same payment amounts.
rules.citation: Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: The Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance requires owners to pay tenants relocation assistance in the event of an owner move-in eviction.

rules.title: 2026 Annual General Adjustment Order (Rent Board Regulation 1148)
rules.requirement: Eligible landlords may raise 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0%, no earlier than January 1, 2026. Landlords must meet the qualifying conditions and give tenants the notice required by Regulation 1148.
rules.coverage_conditions: Eligible landlords of units subject to Berkeley permanent rent ceilings
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to tenancies that began on or after 2025-01-01 where the rent was set under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act.
rules.interaction: Annual implementation of the BMC 13.76.110A formula (the 1.0% equals 65% of the CPI increase). Coexists with the state Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act, which governs initial rents for the excluded tenancies.
rules.citation: Rent Board Regulation 1148; Berkeley Municipal Code section 13.76.110A
rules.quoted_span: eligible landlords to increase the 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0% no earlier than

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance (as amended by Measure BB): Annual General Adjustment
rules.requirement: Landlords of fully covered units may raise rent each year only by the Annual General Adjustment (AGA). The AGA is set at 65% of the increase in the Bay Area CPI-U (measured July 1 to June 30) and may never exceed 5%, even if the formula produces a higher figure.
rules.key_value: AGA = 65% of CPI increase, max 5%
rules.coverage_conditions: Fully covered units, including: most units in multifamily properties built before 1980; single-family homes with current tenancies that began before 1996; rooming houses (single-family homes with 5 or more rooms rented individually under separate leases); and such units with government subsidies (e.g., Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher, Shelter Plus Care, VASH, LIHTC, HOME). Partially covered units are not subject to rent control but remain subject to registration, just cause for eviction, and security deposit interest. Partially covered units are: new construction with a Certificate of Occupancy after June 1980; single-family homes with tenancies beginning on or after 1996-01-01; most condominiums; Section 202/811 units; and Rent Supplement, Section 8 Loan Management Set Aside or Project-based Section 8 units in projects with HUD-insured or HUD-held mortgages.
rules.exemptions: Golden Duplex (owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 and currently owner-occupied in one unit). Units where the tenant shares a kitchen or bath with the owner, if the owner lived on the property when the tenancy began. Tenancies starting after 2018-11-07 on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied. University housing such as dormitories. Nonprofit cooperatives. Landlords with banked (unused) AGAs from prior years may exceed 5% to bring rent up to the rent ceiling.
rules.interaction: Units where federal law, state law or administrative regulation prohibits rent control are only partially covered, so local rent control does not apply to them.
rules.citation: Berkeley Municipal Code section 13.76.110A; Measure BB (Berkeley Rent Ordinance)
rules.quoted_span: The maximum AGA is 5%. This means that, if the formula in the Rent Ordinance results in an AGA that is greater than 5%, the AGA approved by the Board for that year can be no more than 5%.

rules.title: Berkeley Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance (BMC 13.106)
rules.requirement: Rental housing providers may not ask about, require disclosure of, or use criminal history or criminal background checks in advertising, applications, tenant selection, or decisions. This includes refusing to add an immediate family member or disqualifying tenants from rental assistance such as Section 8 based on criminal history. Any adverse action based on criminal history requires written notice and an opportunity to respond, and providers must prominently post the Notice to Rental Applicants and Tenants on application materials, websites, and locations applicants frequently visit.
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental housing providers in Berkeley, with regard to current or prospective tenants
rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing/Section 8 properties; owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record resides in one unit as their primary residence; units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back in per BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates
rules.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance – Security Deposit Interest
rules.requirement: Landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year. If the tenant moves out before the end of the year, the landlord must pay a prorated amount.
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance
rules.exemptions: Golden Duplex; units where the owner shares a kitchen or bath with the tenant, if the owner lived on the property when the tenancy started; tenancies started after Nov 7, 2018 on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied; university rental units such as dormitories; nonprofit cooperatives
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.

rules.title: BMC 13.106 – Criminal History Restrictions (Security Deposits)
rules.requirement: Landlords may not demand a higher security deposit or higher rent based on an applicant's or tenant's criminal history.
rules.coverage_conditions: Current or prospective tenants in Berkeley rental housing
rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing and Section 8 properties; owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record lives in one unit as their primary residence; units under a rental agreement that allows owners to move back in per BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or to add or replace roommates
rules.quoted_span: Demand a higher security deposit or rental amount based on criminal history

rules.title: Boston Housing Stability Notification Act (Sec. 10-11.7)
rules.requirement: A landlord or foreclosing owner who plans to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources at the same time as the Notice to Quit or Notice of Non-renewal of Lease. They must also send the City's Office of Housing Stability a copy of that notice, using the online Submission Verification Form, together with a Certificate of Compliance/Service.
rules.key_value: Penalty: warning for 1st offense; $300/day for 2nd and subsequent offenses
rules.coverage_conditions: All landlords and foreclosing owners intending to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy of a unit in the City of Boston, including when starting an eviction or not offering a lease renewal; former owners after foreclosure must also receive the Notice
rules.exemptions: Residences in any hospital, skilled nursing facility or health facility; residences in a non-profit facility whose primary purpose is short-term treatment, assistance or therapy for alcohol, drug, or other substance abuse. The Ordinance's requirements cannot be waived by lease or agreement; such terms are void.
rules.interaction: This is a notice and reporting requirement only. A violation does not halt the eviction process. The Inspectional Services Department enforces it.
rules.quoted_span: The Housing Stability Notification Act requires any landlord to provide renters with a Notice of Tenant’s Rights and Resources when planning to end a tenancy agreement.

rules.title: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.requirement: Covered housing providers may not use blanket bans on applicants with arrests or convictions. They must review each case individually and may not consider non-conviction arrests, convictions subject to judicial relief such as expungement or sealing, or convictions more than 5 years old when deciding eligibility or eviction. They also may not use credit scores to approve or deny applicants, may use credit history only in place of unavailable rental history, may not reject an applicant for lack of credit history, and must take into account a demonstrated history of paying a higher rent burden.
rules.key_value: Convictions older than 5 years may not be considered
rules.coverage_conditions: Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) funding and/or land, or with income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy; also applied to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program. Covers housing eligibility and eviction decisions.
rules.exemptions: The criminal-history limits do not apply where there is a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought and/or an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to the safety of others, and do not apply to current criminal behavior.
rules.interaction: Preempted by federal or state law where that law imposes a conflicting criminal history requirement.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.quoted_span: Inclusionary Development Policy will not impose a blanket policy that denies

rules.title: Boston fair housing protections (including rental assistance)
rules.requirement: Landlords in Boston may not discriminate in renting housing based on protected characteristics, including race, color, religion, disability, national origin, ancestry, sex, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, marital status, rental assistance, family status, and military status. In particular, landlords may not refuse applicants because they use rental assistance such as Section 8, social security disability, or veterans vouchers.
rules.coverage_conditions: Renting, buying, selling, or securing financing for any housing in the City of Boston.
rules.citation: Boston fair housing protections (including rental assistance)
rules.quoted_span: In the City of Boston, it’s illegal to discriminate when renting, buying, selling, or securing financing for any housing.

rules.title: Cartwright Act – Common Pricing Algorithms (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729, AB 325)
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade in violation of the Cartwright Act. It is also unlawful to use or distribute one while coercing another person to set or adopt a price or commercial term the algorithm recommends for the same or similar products or services in California.
rules.coverage_conditions: Any 'person' as defined in Bus. & Prof. Code § 16702, other than the end consumer. Applies to the price or commercial terms (level of service, availability, output) of any product or service, so it is not limited to rental housing. A common pricing algorithm is any methodology, including computer, software, or other technology, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. Distribution includes selling, licensing, providing access, or subscription.
rules.exemptions: End consumers of a product or service are excluded.
rules.interaction: Part of the state Cartwright Act antitrust framework. The section does not impair or limit the applicability of other antitrust laws, so it coexists with them. Violations are punishable as a crime under the Cartwright Act. The source records give no effective date; the in_force status assumes enactment before the query date. AB 325 was chaptered 2025-10-06 (D022); no explicit date in the text, California non-urgency statutes take effect January 1 of the following year.
rules.citation: Business and Professions Code Section 16729(a)-(b) (AB 325, Chapter 338)
rules.quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

rules.title: California Civil Code § 1950.6 – Application Screening Fees
rules.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to its actual out-of-pocket screening costs, subject to a $30-per-applicant cap adjusted annually by CPI, and may not charge a fee when it knows or should know that no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must offer either a first-come, first-qualified process that charges only applicants actually considered or a full refund to unselected applicants. It must also provide an itemized receipt, refund any unused portion of the fee, and give the applicant a copy of the credit report within 7 days of receiving it.
rules.key_value: Actual out-of-pocket costs, capped at $30 per applicant adjusted annually by CPI since 1998-01-01 ($68.96 maximum for 2026)
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of residential rental property and their agents who charge applicants a screening fee. Applicants include guarantors and cosigners.
rules.exemptions: Under the first-come, first-qualified process, no refund is required for an applicant denied after consideration for failing the established screening criteria.
rules.interaction: State statute. It is not intended to preempt provisions or regulations governing deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs. The effective date comes from the official statute text (D026); D005 gives no date, so there is no conflict.
rules.citation: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6; amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67, Sec. 29 (AB 1170)
rules.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act – Just Cause for Termination of Tenancy (Civ. Code § 1946.2)
rules.requirement: Once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied residential property for 12 months (or 24 months in some cases where adult tenants were added), the owner may terminate the tenancy only for a listed at-fault or no-fault just cause, which must be stated in the written notice. For a no-fault termination, such as owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order, or demolition or substantial remodel, the owner must pay relocation assistance or waive the final month's rent; for a curable lease violation, the owner must first give the tenant an opportunity to cure.
rules.key_value: 12 months continuous occupancy (24 months if adult tenants were added); no-fault relocation assistance or rent waiver equal to one month of the tenant's rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property, including dwellings or units in a mobilehome park. Owner move-in applies to owners who are natural persons as defined in the section. Owners of covered property must give tenants notice of these protections in at least 12-point type.
rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotel occupancy; nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, licensed elderly or adult residential care facilities; school and university dormitories; units where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with a resident owner; single-family owner-occupied residences renting no more than two units or bedrooms; owner-occupied duplexes (neither unit an ADU or JADU); housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome); separately alienable property (for example, single-family homes or condos) not owned by a REIT, a corporation, an LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management, where the required exemption notice was given; deed- or agreement-restricted affordable housing; homeowners of a mobilehome.
rules.interaction: This section does not apply to property covered by a local just cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019, or by a later-adopted or amended ordinance that is more protective; in those cases the local ordinance applies, and a property cannot be subject to both. A less protective local ordinance adopted after September 1, 2019, is unenforceable unless this section is repealed. Relocation assistance under this section is credited against relocation assistance required by any other law. Effective-date note: the records give 2026-01-01 as the effective date, while record 10 states the section became operative April 1, 2024; 2026-01-01 is used here as the date for the current version. The section is repealed as of January 1, 2030.
rules.quoted_span: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.

rules.title: Relocation Payments for Temporary Capital Improvement Displacement (Civ. Code § 1947.9)
rules.requirement: Tenant households temporarily displaced for less than 20 days for capital improvement work must receive a per-day relocation payment plus actual moving expenses, as governed by Civil Code § 1947.9.
rules.key_value: $446.00/day per tenant household plus actual moving expenses for notices served 3/01/26 – 2/28/27 (prior period 3/01/25 – 2/28/26: $436.00/day)
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenant households temporarily displaced for less than 20 days for capital improvement work
rules.interaction: Payments for temporary capital improvement evictions of less than 20 days are governed by state Civil Code § 1947.9 and not by local Rent Ordinance Section 37.9C.
rules.quoted_span: *The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions for less than 20 days is governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 and not by Rent Ordinance Section 37.9C.

rules.title: Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance (Chapter 14.04) – Applicant Selection Standards and Source-of-Income Protection
rules.requirement: Landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to select applicants, such as the applicant's ability to pay rent, care for the apartment and respect the rights of others, but the standard must be applied equally and uniformly to all applicants. Housing discrimination, including in viewing or renting an apartment, is prohibited on the basis of protected categories, including source of income such as Section 8 vouchers and public benefits.
rules.key_value: Civil fines of up to $300 per violation
rules.coverage_conditions: Landlords, sellers and rental agents in Cambridge, and real estate transactions in Cambridge, including viewing or renting an apartment
rules.exemptions: 2-family dwellings where the owner lives there
rules.quoted_span: Under the law, landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to determine which applicants are selected, as long as that standard is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act rent cap (AB 1482, as amended by SB 567), Civil Code Section 1947.12
rules.requirement: Over any 12-month period, an owner of residential real property may not raise the gross rental rate by more than the lower of 5% plus the regional change in cost of living (CPI) or 10%. The base is the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months, excluding accepted discounts or concessions. If the same tenant stays, rent may be raised in no more than two increments in that period. Initial rent for a new tenancy with no prior tenant remaining may be set freely, and any increase requires notice under Civil Code Section 827.
rules.key_value: Lower of 5% + regional CPI or 10% per 12-month period; max 2 increases per 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property, meaning any dwelling or unit intended for human habitation, including units in a mobilehome park. Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (rolling) is excluded, except mobilehomes. For mobilehome tenancies, the cap applies to increases on or after February 18, 2021. Sublease rents may not exceed the allowable rate.
rules.exemptions: Deed- or regulatory-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; dormitories owned and operated by higher-education institutions or K-12 schools; housing under a local rent control that limits annual increases to less than this cap (e.g., units under the City's RSO); housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the past 15 years, unless it is a mobilehome; separately alienable units such as single-family homes or condos not owned by a REIT, a corporation, an LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management, if tenants received the statutory written exemption notice (in the rental agreement for tenancies commenced or renewed on or after 2020-07-01, or 2022-07-01 for mobilehomes), and this exemption does not apply if the lot has more than one dwelling unit or a second unit that cannot be sold separately; an owner-occupied duplex where the owner occupied one unit as a principal residence at the start of the tenancy and continues to live there, and neither unit is an ADU or JADU; homeowners of a mobilehome as defined in Section 798.9.
rules.interaction: Coexists with local rent control: the cap does not apply to housing under a valid local rent control that restricts increases below it. The section neither expands nor limits local authority to regulate rents consistent with Civil Code Chapter 2.7 (commencing with Section 1954.50). The 2024-04-01 date reflects the SB 567 version; transition rules roll back excess increases made between 2019-03-15 and 2020-01-01 (or 2021-02-18 and 2022-01-01 for mobilehomes). Published regional maximums were 8.8% (2023-08-01 to 2024-07-31) and 8.9% (2024-08-01 to 2025-07-31); both periods have expired. Enforcement: tenant civil action for the excess rent, attorney's fees, and up to treble damages for willful conduct; AG, city attorney, or county counsel enforcement; three-year limitations period. Waivers are void.
rules.citation: Civil Code Section 1947.12; Stats. 2023, Ch. 290 (SB 567); AB 1482 (Tenant Protection Act of 2019)
rules.quoted_span: an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.

rules.title: California Civil Code § 1950.6 – Application screening criteria, first-come processing, and reusable screening reports
rules.requirement: A landlord must accept a reusable tenant screening report if the applicant provides one. A landlord charging a screening fee under the § 1950.6(c)(2)(A) process must give its screening criteria in writing with the application, consider completed applications in the order received, and approve the first applicant who meets the criteria.
rules.key_value: First applicant meeting the written screening criteria must be approved
rules.coverage_conditions: Landlords screening prospective tenants. The first-come provisions apply to landlords charging an application screening fee under the § 1950.6(c)(2)(A) process.
rules.interaction: Coexists with FEHA (Gov. Code § 12955) screening restrictions. The 2026-01-01 effective date is sourced for the (c)(2)(A) first-come provisions only. No effective date was given for the reusable screening report provision.
rules.quoted_span: The landlord’s screening criteria shall be provided to the applicant in writing together with the application form.

rules.title: Fair Employment and Housing Act – Criminal history screening limits
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not consider arrests that did not lead to a conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile justice records, and may not impose blanket bans on people with a criminal history. A denial based on a conviction must be directly related to the applicant's ability to be a good tenant without threatening the health and safety of others or the property, taking into account the nature and severity of the crime and the time elapsed since the conduct.
rules.coverage_conditions: Housing providers screening applicants or denying applications based on criminal history
rules.interaction: Part of FEHA. Coexists with the general FEHA housing nondiscrimination rules and with Civ. Code § 1950.6.
rules.quoted_span: Housing  providers cannot consider some types of criminal history including arrests that did not lead to a conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system.

rules.title: FEHA Housing Discrimination – Gov. Code § 12955 (protected characteristics, source of income, inquiries, advertising, aggregate income)
rules.requirement: Owners and other housing providers, including third-party tenant screening companies, may not discriminate in screening or renting based on a protected characteristic, including source of income such as Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers, SSI, and rent relief. They also may not inquire about protected characteristics, publish discriminatory advertisements, or use an income standard that fails to count the combined income of persons residing together on the same basis as married persons.
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of any housing accommodation, landlords, tenant screening companies, property management companies, and other housing providers. Source of income means lawful, verifiable income paid directly to a tenant or a tenant's representative, or paid to a landlord on the tenant's behalf, including public assistance and housing subsidies.
rules.exemptions: An owner occupying a home and renting to one additional person may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics, but may not make, print, or publish discriminatory statements, notices, or advertisements. A written or oral inquiry about the level or source of income is not source-of-income discrimination.
rules.interaction: Coexists with Civ. Code § 1950.6. The subsidy-specific income and credit rules in § 12955(o) are listed separately.
rules.citation: Gov. Code § 12955(a), (b), (c), (n), (p); Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA)
rules.quoted_span: For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.

rules.title: Gov. Code § 12955(o) (SB 267) – Income standards and credit history for subsidized applicants
rules.requirement: Where there is a government rent subsidy, any income standard must be based only on the portion of rent the tenant will pay. A provider may not use credit history unless it offers the applicant the option of lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of ability to pay, such as government benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements. If the applicant provides that evidence, the provider must allow reasonable time to respond and must reasonably consider the evidence in place of credit history.
rules.key_value: Income standard based only on the tenant-paid portion of rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental applications where there is a government rent subsidy

rules.title: Security deposit deductions, inspections, photographs, and return (Civil Code § 1950.5(d)-(n))
rules.requirement: Deductions are limited to amounts reasonably necessary for unpaid rent, tenant-caused damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning to move-in condition, and (if the lease allows) restoring personal property. Pre-existing damage and ordinary wear and tear cannot be charged, and professional cleaning can be charged only if reasonably necessary. The landlord must offer a pre-move-out inspection, photograph the unit as required, and return any remaining deposit with an itemized statement and supporting documentation within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates; security may never be labeled nonrefundable.
rules.key_value: 21 calendar days to return the deposit and itemized statement; statutory damages up to 2x the security for bad-faith retention
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenancies. Move-in photographs are required for tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025. Move-out photographs, taken before and after repairs or cleaning, are required beginning April 1, 2025. If security or rent was paid electronically, the refund must be electronic unless otherwise agreed in writing. With multiple adult tenants, the refund is a check payable to all adult tenants unless there is a written agreement. The landlord's successors in interest must receive the security, or it must be returned to the tenant with an accounting, and successors are jointly and severally liable if this is not done.
rules.exemptions: Supporting documentation is not required when repair and cleaning deductions total $125 or less, or when the tenant signs a valid waiver, unless the tenant requests documentation within 14 days. The inspection notice requirement does not apply to tenancies terminated under Code of Civil Procedure § 1161(2), (3), or (4), and the 48-hour notice may be waived in writing by both parties. A good-faith successor is not liable for statutory damages.
rules.interaction: Same state statute as the deposit limit; this is the return and deduction regime. Some sub-provisions phased in on 2025-01-01 (proof of completed repairs), 2025-04-01 (move-out photographs), and 2025-07-01 (move-in photographs).

rules.interaction: State statute; FEHA anti-discrimination limits on deposit terms also apply. The service-member higher-security provision (§ 1950.5(c)(4)) took effect 2025-04-01.

rules.title: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11: Nonpayment Termination of Written Lease
rules.requirement: If a tenant under a written lease does not pay rent, the landlord may end the lease with 14 days' written notice to quit. The lease is not ended if the tenant pays all rent due, plus interest and costs, by the day the answer is due in the possession action. rules.title: New Jersey algorithmic rent-setting coordination prohibition (P.L. 2026, c.43, §4)
rules.requirement: Rental property owners and their agents may not pay for or use the services of a coordinator, meaning anyone running algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that performs a coordinating function. No person may perform a coordinating function, facilitate anticompetitive agreements among owners, or engage in parallel pricing coordination on reasonably interchangeable residential units.
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of one or more rental residential dwelling units in New Jersey, plus their agents, representatives and subcontractors. A person with a controlling interest in an owning entity counts as a single owner with that entity. The act also covers coordinators, their agents, representatives and subcontractors, and any other person, including corporations, partnerships, trusts and associations.
rules.exemptions: The following do not count as a coordinator or a coordinating function: government entities that set or limit rents through affordability controls, and pricing required by those controls; research, statistical analysis or testing not used to set or recommend prices or terms; rent estimates offered to the public at no cost; and real estate brokerage databases available on equal terms that neither set or recommend prices nor collect competitively sensitive information. An algorithmic device does not include a spreadsheet that runs without AI and requires human analysis, or a database that only queries unprocessed data.

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement: A residential landlord may not evict a tenant or refuse to renew a lease, written or oral, without one of the statutory good causes, and must prove that cause in court. Each ground has its own Notice to Quit period.

Notice to Quit periods: none for nonpayment (14 days in federally subsidized housing); 3 days for conduct and criminal grounds; 1 month for rule, lease, rent-increase and late-payment grounds; 2 months for owner occupancy or sale; 3 months for health and safety or illegal occupancy; 18 months for retirement from residential use; 3 years for condo or co-op conversion. Relocation assistance of 6x monthly rent for illegal-occupancy evictions. Owner must occupy a recovered unit for at least 6 months. Residential use barred for 5 years after a board-up, demolition or retirement eviction.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied premises with two or three units and no more than two rental units; transient or seasonal guests of hotels, motels or guest houses (unless they have no alternate residence); units held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member. The drug-offense ground does not apply if the person is completing or has completed drug rehabilitation.

rules.title: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance (Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance)
rules.requirement: After 30 days of tenancy, an owner may not end a residential tenancy without just cause, which must be stated in a written notice. Just cause includes at-fault reasons (nonpayment of rent, material lease breach, nuisance, criminal activity) and no-fault reasons (owner move-in, removal from the rental market, demolition or substantial remodel). Before serving an at-fault termination notice, the owner must first give the tenant notice of the violation and time to fix it. For a no-fault termination, the owner must either pay 3 months of relocation assistance or waive rent for the final 3 months.
rules.key_value: Applies after 30 days of tenancy; no-fault: 3 months relocation assistance or 3 months rent waiver
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenancies in Santa Ana
rules.exemptions: Housing produced in the last 15 years; deed-restricted affordable housing; hotel and transient occupancy; hospital and care facilities; dormitories; other shared living quarters
rules.interaction: One source (D084) names the instrument 'Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance'. It is treated here as the same local ordinance.
rules.citation: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: After 30 days, an owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in a written notice.

rules.title: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance – Annual Rent Increase Cap
rules.requirement: Landlords may raise residential rent once a year by no more than the lower of 3% or 80% of the CPI change over the most recent 12 months, and by nothing if CPI is negative. The City publishes the allowable increase by June 30 each year, effective September 1. For September 1, 2026 through August 31, 2027 the maximum is 2.87%.
rules.key_value: Lesser of 3% or 80% of CPI change (0% if CPI negative); 2.87% for 2026-09-01 to 2027-08-31
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental property and mobile home spaces in Santa Ana
rules.exemptions: Residential buildings constructed after February 1, 1995; mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990. Owners may petition the City Manager or designee for an increase above the cap if needed for a fair and reasonable return; a decision is due within 60 days of a complete application.
rules.quoted_span: Increase in residential rents are limited to the lower of 3% per year, or 80% of the percent change in the Consumer Price Index over the most recent 12-month period. If the CPI is negative, no rent increase is permitted.
